title: Deserialize JsonPatch
background:
Many JsonPatch workflows start from text received over HTTP or stored as JSON. In JsonPatch.Net, you deserialize that text into a `JsonPatch` instance and inspect its operation list before applying it. This gives application code a chance to validate or log the patch payload before touching domain data.

This lesson focuses on using `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<JsonPatch>(...)` and the `Operations` collection. The goal is to produce a small summary object from the deserialized patch so you can confirm the document was parsed and recognized correctly by the library.
instructions: Deserialize the patch text into `JsonPatch`, then return a summary object with `operationCount` and `firstOperation`.

title: Apply To JsonNode
background:
Once a patch is parsed, the most direct library workflow is `patch.Apply(document)`. JsonPatch.Net returns a `PatchResult` object rather than throwing for common patch failures, so your code can inspect both transformed output and failure state in one place.

In this lesson, you will execute a patch against a `JsonNode` input and return the patched value. This isolates the core apply call that most integrations use before adding error handling or typed-model behavior.
instructions: Apply the parsed patch to the input document and return the patched JSON result.

title: Choose Operation Factories
background:
JsonPatch.Net provides factory methods on `PatchOperation` for operations such as `Add`, `Replace`, `Move`, `Copy`, and `Test`. In application code, you choose the methods that match a concrete patch goal, then compose those operations into a single `JsonPatch`.

This lesson focuses on that composition step. You will build one patch that first verifies status with `Test`, then updates status with `Replace`, and finally copies `name` into `displayName` with `Copy`.
instructions: Build a patch that verifies `status` is `draft`, replaces `status` with `published`, and copies `name` to `displayName`. Apply it and return the patched document.

title: Use PatchResult For Errors
background:
A key integration detail in JsonPatch.Net is that apply failures are reported through `PatchResult` rather than by defaulting to exception-driven flow. This gives you a predictable branch point for application logic and lets you return user-friendly messages without wrapping every apply call in broad catch blocks.

This lesson focuses on observing `PatchResult.Error` and `PatchResult.IsSuccess` after `Apply`. You will return a small status object that reports whether the operation succeeded and includes an error message only when the patch could not be applied.
instructions: Apply the patch and return `{ status, error }`, using `PatchResult` to report either `applied` or `failed`.

title: Apply To Typed Model With Options
background:
JsonPatch.Net also supports patching typed .NET models through extension overloads. In that workflow, serializer configuration matters because patch paths are resolved against the serialized property names produced by your `JsonSerializerOptions`.

This lesson uses the typed apply overload that accepts `JsonSerializerOptions`. You will deserialize a model, apply a patch with camel-case naming, and return serialized output so path-to-property mapping behavior is explicit.
instructions: Apply the patch to the typed `Person` model using serializer options, then return the updated model as JSON.

title: Create Patch From JsonNode
background:
JsonPatch.Net can generate patch documents by diffing start and target JSON values. This is useful when your application computes desired state and wants a compact patch payload to store, transmit, or apply later.

This lesson focuses on the `CreatePatch` extension for `JsonNode` values. You will generate the patch from two inputs and return the serialized patch document to inspect which operations the library produced.
instructions: Generate a patch from `start` to `target` using the JsonNode `CreatePatch` extension and return the patch JSON.

title: Create Patch From Typed Models
background:
Patch generation is also available for typed object graphs through generic extension overloads. This lets your application work in domain types first, then produce patch documents from model-to-model differences without manual operation construction.

In this lesson, you will use the typed `CreatePatch<T>` overload with serializer options. The focus is selecting the typed diff-generation API and returning the generated patch document for inspection.
instructions: Generate a patch between typed `Person` values using `CreatePatch<T>` with serializer options, then return the patch JSON.

title: Create And Apply Round Trip
background:
A common utility workflow is to generate a patch from a start and target document, then immediately apply that patch in memory to verify behavior. This confirms your model-to-patch transformation and apply pipeline are aligned before persisting or transmitting the patch.

This lesson combines those two library surfaces in a constrained round-trip utility: generate with `CreatePatch`, apply with `Apply`, and return both operation count and transformed output. The emphasis is orchestration of JsonPatch.Net APIs in one practical function.
instructions: Generate a patch from `start` to `target`, apply it to a clone of `start`, and return `{ operationCount, document }`.
